rules.title: Novelty Requirement Under AIA §102(a)(1)
rules.requirement: A person shall be entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
exceptions: Grace period: Disclosures made within 1 year before filing by the inventor or by one who obtained the subject matter from the inventor do not constitute prior art (§102(b)(1))

rules.title: Anticipation Standard — All Elements
rules.requirement: A claim is anticipated under §102 only if each and every element of the claim is found, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference. It is NOT permitted to combine references to establish anticipation — that is an obviousness (§103) analysis.
exceptions: A reference that incorporates another by reference effectively becomes a single reference for anticipation purposes

examples.compliant: Reference D1 explicitly describes elements A, B, C, and D of the claim in a single embodiment — claim is anticipated.
examples.non_compliant: Reference D1 shows A+B, reference D2 shows C+D — combining them is §103 obviousness, not §102 anticipation.

rules.title: Inherent Anticipation
rules.requirement: A prior art reference may anticipate a claim even without explicitly disclosing a feature, if that feature is necessarily present (inherent) in the reference's disclosure. The inherent feature must inevitably result from the disclosed process or composition — mere possibility is insufficient.
exceptions: The inherent feature need not be recognized or appreciated by the prior art author
Inherency cannot be based on what might result — only on what MUST result

examples.compliant: Prior art describes alloy with exact composition X — the inevitable crystal structure is inherently disclosed even if not mentioned.
examples.non_compliant: Prior art describes a general process that might sometimes produce product Y — this is not inherent anticipation.

rules.reference: MPEP §2112; Schering Corp. v. Geneva Pharms., 339 F.3d 1373

rules.title: Printed Publication as Prior Art
rules.requirement: A reference qualifies as a 'printed publication' if it was sufficiently accessible to the public interested in the art. Factors include: indexing in a library, availability on the internet, distribution at a conference, or accessibility through commercial databases.
exceptions: A thesis stored in a university library is a printed publication if it is catalogued and publicly accessible
A document with restricted access (under NDA, internal corporate memo) is NOT a printed publication

rules.title: AIA §102(a)(2) — Earlier-Filed Applications
rules.requirement: A claimed invention is unpatentable if it was described in a patent or published application naming another inventor, filed before the effective filing date. This includes provisionals (for their disclosure content), PCT applications designating the US, and granted patents.
exceptions: §102(b)(2) exceptions: (A) disclosure obtained from inventor, (B) prior public disclosure by inventor, (C) common ownership/obligation to assign before filing

rules.title: Effective Filing Date
rules.requirement: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is the earlier of: (a) the actual filing date of the application, or (b) the filing date of a prior application to which priority/benefit is claimed, if the prior application provides written description support for the claim under §112(a).

examples.compliant: Application filed 2025-06-01 claims priority to provisional filed 2024-06-01 which fully supports the claims — effective filing date is 2024-06-01.
examples.non_compliant: Priority claimed to a provisional that does not describe the specific claimed embodiment — effective filing date remains the actual filing date.

rules.title: Genus-Species / Broad-Narrow Claims
rules.requirement: A prior art reference disclosing a species anticipates a genus claim encompassing that species. Conversely, a generic disclosure does NOT normally anticipate a specific species claim unless the species is clearly identified.
exceptions: A small genus (e.g., 3-4 members explicitly listed) may anticipate any one member
A 'picture claim' describing exactly the prior art embodiment is anticipated

examples.compliant: Prior art discloses 'sodium chloride solution at 0.9%' — this anticipates a generic claim to 'saline solutions' encompassing 0.9% NaCl.
examples.non_compliant: Prior art generically discloses 'halide salts' — a specific claim to 'potassium iodide at pH 7.2' is not anticipated.

rules.title: Enablement of Anticipating Reference
rules.requirement: A prior art reference must enable the subject matter it describes in order to anticipate. If a person skilled in the art could not make or use the disclosed invention without undue experimentation, the reference does not qualify as anticipating prior art.
exceptions: The reference need not enable the CLAIMED invention — only its own disclosure

review_checklist: Does each anticipation rejection identify a SINGLE reference containing ALL claim elements?
Is the effective filing date correctly determined (considering priority/provisional)?
Is the 1-year grace period properly accounted for (inventor's own disclosures)?
For inherent anticipation — is the feature shown to NECESSARILY result (not merely possibly)?
Is the prior art reference properly qualified (printed publication, patent, public use)?
For genus-species issues — is the direction of anticipation correct?
Does the anticipating reference enable its own disclosure?
Are §102(a)(2) prior art exceptions (common ownership, prior inventor disclosure) checked?
Is each claim element mapped to a specific passage in the reference?
system_prompt_injection: You are a senior USPTO patent examiner assessing novelty under 35 U.S.C. §102 (AIA). Apply the strict 'all elements' test: every limitation of the claim must be found in a SINGLE prior art reference, either expressly or inherently. Never combine references for a §102 rejection — that belongs under §103. Check the effective filing date carefully (priority claims, provisionals). Apply the 1-year grace period where the inventor's own disclosure predates filing. For inherent anticipation, the feature must necessarily be present — possibility is not enough. Map each claim element to a specific passage in the reference.
